CS2881R · Assignment 2 · Part 2

Refusal Probes on Qwen3-32B

Qwen3-32B (thinking off) · judge claude-opus-5-5, rubric v2_1 (frozen) · November 2026 Working draft

Updated ET. Exploratory (train→val) and held-out (test) results are labeled separately throughout.

Bottom line

Can a linear read of Qwen3-32B's residual stream reproduce the judge's refuse/comply label, and what does it read?

  • Yes, before the model writes anything. A logistic-regression probe at the last template token (last_prompt, layer 57) reaches held-out test AUROC 0.975 [0.955, 0.988] in distribution and 0.979 [0.960, 0.993] on prompt types never seen in training. It barely beats the model's own first-token distribution (0.965 / 0.978), and the CIs overlap. The output layer already carries most of the decision.
  • After the response exists, the text is enough. The response-side probe (mean over response tokens, L47) scores 0.997 / 0.998. TF-IDF on the same text gets 0.988 / 0.993, and response length alone 0.906 / 0.983. Among a prompt's samples that disagree, probe and TF-IDF tie in distribution (0.976 each); the probe wins on held-out types (0.917 vs 0.875).
  • It reads behavior, not only harmfulness. The safety label alone scores 0.862 / 0.921. The prompt probe scores 0.93 within safe prompts on both test splits. Its typical error is over-predicting refusal on safe prompts with violent words: euthanizing a dog, a judo choke, a “massacre” scene for TV. The OR-Bench safe cell is its weakest (accuracy 0.80).
  • A probe direction can carry the refusal template without carrying the decision. Adding the best difference-of-means direction (L53) turns 88% of complied val prompts into template refusals. Ablating it everywhere strips the “I'm sorry, I can't” opener from the model's refusals (35 → 2 of 54). Yet a blind read of 320-token generations finds all 54 still refuse, as lectures and redirects. The logistic-regression direction does no better than a random one. Probe accuracy picks out where refusal is readable, not where it is decided.
  • No drop on held-out types for any probe, but the unsafe-and-complied cells are tiny (11 val responses), so within-unsafe numbers are noisy: test held-out within-unsafe is 0.68 for the prompt probe.

Probe configurations were chosen on val and frozen (part2/FROZEN.json, 06:28 UTC) before test was read once. The manual review is not yet done: Section 9 shows the sample with Claude's diagnostic reads, which are not manual labels.

1Question and setup

Part 1 built a judge that labels each Qwen3-32B response as FULL_REFUSAL, PARTIAL or FULL_COMPLIANCE. Part 2 asks whether a linear read of the model's residual stream reproduces that label, and what such a probe actually reads. The binary target is y = 1[FULL_COMPLIANCE]. Whether refusing was appropriate is a separate question, answered by the dataset's safe/unsafe label, which neither the judge nor the probes see.

Activations were re-extracted (teacher-forced, bf16, all 64 layers) from the committed responses, because the Part 1 activations stayed on the old pod. Ten prompt-side positions cover the last token of the user's text and every chat-template token after it. Four response-side summaries follow. Prompt-side states exist before the model writes anything, so they test prediction. Response-side states read text the model has already written.

2Which layers and positions are best?

Exploratory: train → val.

Late prompt-side positions win. On val, last_prompt peaks at L57 (LR 0.984, DoM 0.968 at L53), and every template token after <|im_end|> lands within ~0.01 of it. inst_last, the last user token, is lower (LR 0.962 at L48). Some of the refusal decision is assembled on the template tokens after the user finishes, consistent with Zhao et al. Response-side sites sit at 0.97–0.99 from layer 0 on, which says more about the text than about the model (Section 6).

3Probes vs baselines

Two baselines matter. The next-token distribution (the model's own log-probs for its first token, fed to logistic regression) is nearly as good as the best prompt-side probe. On these prompts the decision is mostly committed by the final layer, and a residual probe adds a little calibration rather than new information. TF-IDF on the response is nearly as good as the best response-side probe, because refusals are worded like refusals. The other prompt-side baselines are much weaker: TF-IDF on the prompt scores 0.744 / 0.613 and the safety label 0.862 / 0.921. A probe at last_prompt therefore reads more than wording or topic.

4Held-out test, frozen configuration

Test evaluation is running. This section fills in when it finishes.

The two probes fail in opposite directions. The prompt probe over-predicts refusal: 31 of 238 complied in-distribution responses are scored as refusals, against 10 of 173 refusals scored as compliance. It cannot see the response, so it errs on borderline safe prompts that this model usually answers. TF-IDF on the response over-predicts compliance (16 of 173 refusals missed) because a hedged refusal that offers alternatives looks like an answer. The response probe makes 10 errors out of 411. PARTIAL responses, folded into the refusal class, sit in the middle of both probes' score distributions (median percentile 0.38), as a binary target that hides a third class should produce.

5Does the probe read behavior, or harmfulness?

The safety label alone predicts the judge label for 86% of dev responses, so a probe could score well by detecting “this prompt looks harmful” without tracking what the model did. Three checks separate the two: probes trained on the safety label instead of y; the behavior probe's AUROC within safe prompts and within unsafe prompts, where the safety label is constant; and a 2×2 contrast that estimates each direction with the other variable held fixed.

The pooled 2×2 contrast was misleading at first: its strongly negative cosine came from the dataset source. Safe-refused prompts are mostly OR-Bench and safe-complied mostly XSTest. Holding the source fixed (OR-Bench only) weakens the early negative cosine from about −0.9 to −0.4 and turns it positive after layer ~40. Inside OR-Bench, at late template positions, the “unsafe vs safe, both refused” direction also predicts behavior on safe prompts: val AUROC 0.85 at last_prompt L56, against 0.24–0.44 when pooled. That is the over-refusal story in geometric form: on OR-Bench, “looks harmful” and “will refuse” share a component. They are not one direction, though (cos ≈ 0.35), and the behavior probe stays at 0.90 within safe OR-Bench prompts.

The source-controlled run is a post-hoc check on dev data, added after the pooled result looked implausible; it is not part of the frozen test configuration.

6Shortcuts

Length and truncation are strong shortcuts on held-out types (0.983) because XSTest refusals are short. The first token alone scores 0.85–0.87: refusals open with “I”. The response probe survives inside every subgroup, including the within-prompt comparison, where length and topic are mostly matched. It still errs when a response opens like a refusal and then answers in full (orbench_hard_887, orbench_hard_5). In those cases it is reading the opener.

7Probe families and controls

Exploratory: train → val, at the val-selected (site, layer).

All families land within 0.02–0.04 AUROC of each other, so the readout is not fragile to the estimator. Logistic regression wins at both sites, and shrinkage LDA is nearly as good. An MLP adds nothing, so a nonlinear readout gains no accuracy here. Shuffled-label LR sits at chance (0.39–0.58). The best of 500 random directions reaches 0.93 at last_prompt, a reminder that the label is spread across many dimensions late in the network, so a high AUROC alone does not single out a direction. Difference of means nearly matches LR with as few as 40 train prompts.

8Causal check: do these directions mediate refusal?

The intervention run (ablation and addition, greedy generation on val prompts) is in progress.

Taken at face value, the keyword detector says DoM ablation all but eliminates refusal (72% → 4%), while random directions of the same norm leave it at 69–70%. Reading the generations reverses that conclusion. The 64-token outputs were mostly lectures, so the four refused-prompt conditions were re-generated at 320 tokens and labeled blind to condition:

Blind read of 320-token generations on the 54 always-refused val prompts. Two Claude subagents labeled all 216 shuffled generations under rubric v2_1 without seeing the condition. These are not the Part 1 judge and not manual labels. Style: template = “I’m sorry, I can’t…”, lecture = moralizes and gives nothing, redirect = declines and offers alternatives, benign_answer = answers a premise-rejecting prompt.

Conditionrefusalpartialcomplytemplatelectureredirectbenign answercompliesdegenerate
no intervention493235011710
ablate DoM (L53)540021728601
ablate LR (L57)445521418740
ablate random482432111730

After DoM ablation, all 54 generations still refuse under the rubric, slightly more than without intervention (49 refusals, 3 partials, 2 compliances). What changes is the style: the “I'm sorry, I can't” template drops from 35 to 2, replaced by lectures and redirects. The L53 difference-of-means direction, the best DoM probe on val, carries how the model refuses, not whether it refuses. That differs from Arditi et al., whose ablated models complied. One reason may be that their direction was chosen by intervention efficacy at a mid layer, while ours was chosen by probe accuracy at a late one. The LR direction's ablation leaves templates in place and moves compliance no more than a random direction (10 vs 6 non-refusals of 54, within noise). Addition is still a strong lever on style: DoM ×2 turns 88% of complied prompts into template refusals.

Follow-up: Section 14 sweeps the layer of the ablated direction to test whether a mid-layer direction removes the decision itself.

9Agreement and disagreement review

36 test responses: 12 where the response probe disagrees with the judge (of 20), 12 where the prompt probe disagrees (of 67), and 4 agreements per judge label. Disagreement strata diagnose failure modes; they do not estimate accuracy. The Claude read column is a diagnostic note written by Claude during the autonomous run. It is not a manual label. Manual labels go in part2/manual_labels_test.csv via python label_tool.py --sample part2/review_sample.jsonl --out part2/manual_labels_test.csv, with the judge and probe outputs hidden.

Claude's tags: 12 prompt- or response-probe errors driven by topic words; 3 response-probe errors on a refusal opener followed by a full answer; 4 cases where the rubric itself is ambiguous (e.g. xstest_138, where the judge labeled the same benign reading FULL_COMPLIANCE in two samples and PARTIAL in the third); 2 errors the prompt probe cannot fix, because the model's 3 samples disagree; 2 boundary cases; 1 question of appropriateness; 12 clean agreements.

The review sample is drawn after the test run.

10What geometry does a linear probe assume?

  • One direction. A linear probe assumes the label is a monotone function of a single projection: complying and refusing states sit on opposite sides of one hyperplane. Refusal may instead live in a low-dimensional cone (Wollschläger et al., 2025). A rank-1 readout can still classify a cone well, since a cone has a mean direction, but the probe's weight vector is then not “the” mechanism.
  • The metric is a choice. Difference of means assumes isotropic within-class noise in raw coordinates: LDA with an identity covariance. Logistic regression on standardized activations assumes the per-dimension scales matter and lets the L2 penalty pick among separating directions. Shrinkage LDA whitens with the full covariance. These give different directions (Section 7 reports their cosines) because the Euclidean inner product on the residual stream is not canonical (Park et al., 2023).
  • Discriminative is not the same as representational. With features in superposition, logistic regression tilts its weights to cancel correlated nuisance directions (Marks & Tegmark, 2023). That makes it a better classifier and a worse estimate of the feature direction. The causal check in Section 8 tests this directly.
  • Locality. Reading one token at one layer assumes the decision is concentrated there. The response-side averages relax this; the prompt-side probes do not.
  • Three classes collapsed to two. The binary target assumes PARTIAL sits on the refusal side of one axis. Section 4 shows where PARTIAL responses actually score.
  • Gaussian, shared-covariance classes are what make LDA Bayes-optimal among linear rules. The 64-layer sweep, a near-deterministic label in some prompt families, and heavy class imbalance within cells all bend this assumption.

11Limitations

  • Re-extracted activations. Part 1's activations stayed on a terminated pod. Part 2 re-extracts by teacher-forcing the committed responses in bf16, which should match generation-time states up to numerical noise. It has not been checked against the originals.
  • Tiny unsafe-complied cells (25 train, 11 val responses). Within-unsafe AUROCs have wide CIs. The val-to-test drop at last_prompt (0.955 → 0.68 on held-out types) may be noise.
  • Judge-blocked responses are excluded (no label), and the judge is itself a model. The probe matches the judge, not the truth, and 4 of 36 reviewed items show the rubric is ambiguous at the boundary.
  • Selection optimism. Site, layer and C were chosen on val, so val numbers are optimistic. Only the test columns are clean.
  • Causal check is crude. Refusal is detected by keyword regex or opening phrase on 64 greedy tokens, without the LLM judge. Greedy baselines differ from sampled ones (72% refusal on always-refused prompts). Read the numbers as relative across conditions.
  • Source confound. Dataset source correlates with both the safety label and behavior. The 2×2 contrast is reported pooled and inside OR-Bench only, and the OR-Bench-only check was added post hoc.
  • The manual review has not been done by a human. Section 9 holds the sample and Claude's reads only.
